title: Career Roadmap: Composite Technician
summary: A Composite Technician manufactures, repairs, inspects and finishes components made from composite materials used in aircraft and aerospace systems. These materials often combine reinforcing fibres, such as carbon fibre or glass fibre, with a resin matrix to create lightweight, strong structures.

facts.Current degree: Aviation & Aerospace Programmes (B.Sc Aviation / CPL Integrated / AME / BBA Aviation)

about.label: Education Pathway
about.text: Aviation & Aerospace Programmes – Aerospace Manufacturing / Maintenance, Repair & Overhaul (MRO)

blocks.text: A Composite Technician manufactures, repairs, inspects and finishes components made from composite materials used in aircraft and aerospace systems. These materials often combine reinforcing fibres, such as carbon fibre or glass fibre, with a resin matrix to create lightweight, strong structures.
Composite materials are used in aircraft panels, fairings, interior structures, control surfaces and other components, depending on the aircraft design.
Composite Technicians follow engineering drawings, material specifications, approved work instructions and quality procedures to ensure components meet required standards.
Key responsibilities

items.text: Prepare composite materials, tools, moulds and work surfaces.
Cut and position fibre reinforcements according to approved layup instructions.
Apply resins and other materials according to specified procedures.
Perform vacuum bagging and support curing processes.
Manufacture and finish composite components.
Conduct dimensional and visual inspections.
Identify defects such as delamination, voids, wrinkles and fibre distortion.
Assist with composite component repairs under approved instructions.
Maintain traceability of materials, batches and manufacturing steps.
Follow workplace safety, environmental and quality-control procedures.
Document work and report non-conformities to authorised personnel.

blocks.text: The precise scope of work depends on the employer, component type, training and authorisation. Aircraft structural repairs must follow approved maintenance data and applicable aviation regulations.
Recommended route after Class 10 or Class 12
The best entry route depends on whether you want to work in aerospace manufacturing, composite fabrication or aircraft maintenance and repair.

rows.text: Build foundations in mathematics, science, measurement and practical technical work.
A science stream with Physics, Chemistry and Mathematics can support further technical study; exact eligibility depends on the course.
Consider aerospace, mechanical, manufacturing, materials, polymer or composite-related programmes.
Learn composite fabrication, material handling, layup, curing, finishing and inspection under supervised conditions.
Gain practical exposure in aerospace manufacturing, composite fabrication or an eligible MRO environment.
Apply for composite technician, composite fabrication trainee or aerospace production technician roles.

blocks.text: Relevant qualifications
Potential pathways include:

items.text: Diploma in Mechanical Engineering
Diploma in Aerospace or Aeronautical Engineering
Diploma in Manufacturing Engineering
B.Tech / B.E. in Aerospace or Aeronautical Engineering
B.Tech / B.E. in Mechanical or Materials Engineering
Specialised composite manufacturing or polymer technology training
Employer-led aerospace manufacturing and composite fabrication programmes

blocks.text: A degree is not required for every technician vacancy. Some employers accept relevant diplomas, vocational qualifications or demonstrated practical competencies.

blocks.label: Important distinction
blocks.text: Composite manufacturing and aircraft maintenance are related but not identical. If the role involves regulated aircraft maintenance or certifying maintenance work, additional licensing, approval and experience requirements may apply. Confirm the requirements of the specific employer and relevant aviation authority.
The following is an illustrative study plan for a student entering a relevant diploma or degree programme.
Year 1
Foundation
Learn materials and manufacturing fundamentals

items.text: Study engineering mathematics, physics and basic mechanics.
Understand metals, polymers, fibres and composite materials.
Learn technical drawing, measurements and engineering tolerances.
Practise workshop safety and technical documentation.
Develop basic computer and spreadsheet skills.

blocks.text: Year 2
Materials
Understand composite structures and fabrication

items.text: Study carbon fibre, glass fibre, aramid fibres and resin systems.
Learn composite layup concepts and fibre orientation.
Understand mould preparation, vacuum bagging and curing principles.
Study defects, dimensional inspection and material traceability.
Practise reading manufacturing drawings and work instructions.

blocks.text: Year 3
Application
Develop practical fabrication skills

items.text: Participate in supervised composite fabrication exercises.
Learn trimming, drilling, edge finishing and dimensional verification.
Study quality documentation and non-conformance reporting.
Gain exposure to ultrasonic or other inspection methods through authorised training.
Complete an internship or project in a relevant manufacturing environment.

blocks.text: Final year
Readiness
Prepare for aerospace technician employment

items.text: Complete a project involving composite fabrication or quality inspection.
Learn the importance of approved processes and component traceability.
Practise interpreting drawings, layup schedules and process documentation.
Prepare examples demonstrating safe working and defect identification.
Apply for composite technician and aerospace production trainee positions.

rows.text: Fibre types, resin systems, laminates and sandwich structures
Storage, shelf life, batch identification and handling requirements
Ply orientation, stacking sequences and preparation of reinforcements
Bagging materials, vacuum integrity and process documentation
Temperature, pressure, time and process-control principles
Trimming, edge finishing, drilling and dimensional checks
Delamination, voids, wrinkles, porosity and fibre distortion
Dimensions, tolerances, layup schedules and manufacturing instructions
Inspection records, traceability and non-conformance reporting
PPE, chemical handling, ventilation and dust-control procedures

blocks.text: Technicians must follow the material manufacturer's instructions and approved process specifications. Composite manufacturing parameters should never be improvised on aerospace components.
Carbon fibre composites
Known for high stiffness and strength relative to weight. Used in selected aircraft structural components and aerospace applications.
Glass fibre composites
Used in many industrial and aerospace applications where their mechanical, electrical or cost characteristics are suitable.
Resins and prepregs
Learn how resin systems bind fibres together, how prepreg materials are handled and why storage conditions and out-of-life material controls matter.
Sandwich structures
Understand how thin composite skins and lightweight cores form panels with useful stiffness and weight characteristics.
A composite technician may encounter the following equipment, depending on the workplace:

items.text: Cutting tools and templates for fibre reinforcement.
Moulds, release materials and layup tools.
Vacuum pumps, bagging films, sealants and vacuum gauges.
Curing ovens or autoclaves operated under approved procedures.
Precision measuring tools and dimensional inspection equipment.
Trimming and drilling tools with appropriate dust extraction.
Visual inspection aids and approved non-destructive testing equipment.
Material storage systems and temperature-monitoring equipment.
Manufacturing records, digital work instructions and traceability systems.

blocks.text: Some equipment requires specific training and authorisation. Vacuum systems, curing equipment, chemicals and composite dust can create safety hazards if handled incorrectly.
Quality is critical because defects may affect the performance and structural integrity of aerospace components.

rows.text: Air pockets or gaps within a laminate
Distortion or folding of reinforcement fibres
Deviation from the specified fibre orientation
Incorrect resin distribution in a laminate
A component that does not meet drawing tolerances
Missing or inconsistent batch, expiry or process records

blocks.text: Technicians should identify, document and escalate defects according to established procedures. They should not independently approve structural defects or repairs outside their authorised responsibilities.
Useful areas of training include:

rows.text: Understanding storage, contamination prevention and material preparation
Safe handling of resins, hardeners, solvents and cleaning products
Reducing exposure to composite dust and chemical substances
Understanding approved operating and safety procedures
Following controlled work instructions and recording process data
Maintaining material, batch and manufacturing records
Understanding inspection principles and when specialist inspection is required
Recognising fatigue, procedural errors and the importance of disciplined work

blocks.text: Seek training from recognised technical institutes, employers or approved providers. Verify whether a certificate is accepted for the specific vacancy rather than assuming it is an industry-wide requirement.

sections.heading: Projects to Build a Strong Portfolio

blocks.text: Complete three projects that demonstrate material knowledge, process discipline and quality awareness. Use non-flight-critical educational samples and approved workshop facilities.

blocks.label: Project 1
blocks.text: Composite Laminate Study
Compare educational laminate samples made from different fibre orientations or reinforcement types under supervised conditions.

blocks.label: Deliverables
blocks.text: material comparison, process record, visual observations and discussion of limitations.

blocks.label: Project 2
blocks.text: Vacuum Bagging Process Documentation
Study an approved training exercise and document its preparation, materials, inspection checkpoints and process records.

blocks.label: Deliverables
blocks.text: process flowchart, checklist, sample log and safety assessment.

blocks.label: Project 3
blocks.text: Composite Defect Classification
Build a reference catalogue of common composite defects using training samples, authorised images or published technical references.

blocks.label: Deliverables
blocks.text: defect identification guide, inspection checklist and sample non-conformance report.
Do not perform experimental repairs on aircraft parts or flight-critical structures. Any hands-on project should use suitable training materials, approved instructions and appropriate supervision.

Progression depends on practical expertise, quality performance, additional training and employer requirements. Engineering and certification roles may require qualifications beyond those expected of a technician.
Composite technicians may find opportunities in:

Carbon fibre component manufacturing
Aerospace component repair and inspection

Automated composite manufacturing

blocks.text: Developing skills in material science, quality documentation, inspection technology and disciplined manufacturing practices can help broaden career options.

For a student aiming to become a Composite Technician, the most practical route is to develop a strong foundation in materials and manufacturing, obtain relevant technical training, and gain supervised hands-on experience with composite fabrication and inspection.

Prioritise composite materials, layup methods, vacuum bagging, curing principles, defect identification, quality documentation and workplace safety. Seek internships or trainee roles where you can learn controlled manufacturing processes and work with experienced technicians.

The key to success is precision, process discipline and safety. In aerospace manufacturing, every material batch, process step and inspection record matters because component quality can directly affect aircraft safety and reliability.
